title_en: Is Western Welfare Built on Six Centuries of Global Plunder?
excerpt_en: Every time someone says Western welfare was paid for by six hundred years of plunder, Sweden comes out to slap that down. No colonies, no empire — just education, pensions, and a state that decided to serve its people.
body_en:
"Western democracies with elected governments — is their high welfare today built on six hundred years of global plunder since the Age of Discovery?" Is that true?

Every time this comes up, I love letting Sweden slap it down.

High welfare funded by a global colonial empire: wrong. Welfare spending inevitably leads to economic stagnation and ends up like Argentina: wrong. It's not that we won't give welfare, it's that we must wait until the country is rich: wrong.

Look back at Sweden's hundred-year journey. It is like a quiet, hardworking, honest man of the North: knowing it had few people, it quietly valued education, quietly valued every person, and quietly raised social welfare step by step — until, almost without noticing, it became one of the most developed countries in the world.

What is hardest to hold back a laugh about is that Sweden was not an honest man from the start. It was once an empire chasing expansion, and only after several crushing defeats did it finally face reality.

The Great Northern War of 1700–1721 ended in Sweden's defeat, and Sweden lost its hegemony in the Baltic region. In 1809, Sweden lost Finland to Russia in another war.

Sweden's path of national development changed as a result: it gradually shifted from military expansion to economic construction, and after 1814 it avoided getting drawn into large-scale European wars for a long time.

In 1842, Sweden introduced compulsory elementary education, requiring every parish and town to set up schools, with the state responsible for training teachers. The Swedish parliament's historical records state it plainly: all children will get an education.

Then, in the second half of the 19th century, Sweden began to industrialize, relying mainly on its own iron ore, forests, and water power, along with railways, machinery manufacturing, and export trade. Railways and telegraphs connected the country, and industrial enterprises gradually grew.

But industrialization brought new social problems: harsh living conditions for workers, long working hours, and a widening gap between rich and poor. Sweden at that time was far from the Sweden of today. Official historical estimates say that from the mid-19th century to 1930, about 1.3 million Swedes emigrated abroad.

The turning point came more than a hundred years ago.

In 1909, men gained universal suffrage; in 1921, women voted in parliamentary elections for the first time, and equal voting rights for men and women were formally established. That meant political power in the country began shifting from a minority into the hands of all adult citizens.

Then parliament passed the 1913 Swedish pension reform — the world's first universal public insurance system. For the first time, Sweden had pension insurance covering a broad population. The benefits were still very low, of course, but at least it was a first step.

It's not that we won't give welfare, it's that we must wait until the country is rich: wrong.

You don't need to wait until the country is rich to start giving welfare, because not every citizen will live long enough to see that day.

Then came an even more momentous shift: in the 1930s, from "the nation needs the people" to "the nation serves the people."

The most representative idea of the Swedish welfare state is the "People's Home" (Folkhemmet), proposed by the Social Democratic Party. The concept was first put forward in 1928 by the Social Democratic leader Per Albin Hansson. In his speech he said: In a good home, there are no privileged people and no neglected people; no favorites and no stepchildren.

That was not praise for Sweden at the time. He went on to criticize: although political rights were tending toward equality, class differences and economic inequality still existed, and democracy had to be extended further into social and economic life.

The idea stressed that the nation should be like a family, where every member receives basic security.

After the People's Home was proposed, Sweden began building a more complete social security system in the 1930s. In 1938, trade unions and employers' organizations reached the Saltsjöbaden Agreement, laying the foundation for labor-management cooperation. After the war, Sweden further expanded social welfare, public education, health care, and housing construction.

For example, Sweden established a statutory right to two weeks of paid vacation as early as 1938.

Readers who have made it this far can compare and ask themselves two questions: Do you have two weeks of paid vacation? And which has higher per capita productivity — China today, or Sweden in 1938?

By now, modern Sweden had basically taken shape. You all know the rest of the story.

To close, I want to rest the camera on a single moment in the long life of an ordinary Swede:

Maja was born in 1918 and grew up in a mining community near Karlskoga. She attended school for only six years. She had five children, divorced in 1957, and supported her family for years with cleaning work and odd jobs. In 1970, she collected her diaries and published "Report from a Scrub Bucket" (Rapport från en skurhink). At the start of the book, Maja recalls waiting four hours with her children at a clinic, then pushing a heavy twin stroller home. The children were fussy, she was exhausted, and going uphill she even felt nauseous. Just as she was almost home, a neighbor on a bicycle stopped and told her she could apply for social assistance, repeating emphatically: You have every right to it... It is the law.

Her twin sons had strabismus and needed specialist checks. A few days later, she went to the office for the first time and received a voucher: "This doctor's visit will be paid for by the office." After that the children saw doctors many times, using glasses and eye-patching treatment; according to her account, by age six the affected eye's vision had been corrected.

I hope that one day our country, too, can be like Sweden sixty years ago — where a kind passerby can say to people in hardship, whether a struggling mother, an unemployed father, or a poor person struck by serious illness: "Go apply for social assistance. You have every right to it... It is the law."
